item.title: Air Canada targets global growth with new routes, while U.S. travel demand still sags
item.description: Air Canada is embarking on a major expansion of its overseas network, announcing seven new routes in Europe and Asia.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — Air Canada is embarking on a major expansion of its overseas network, announcing seven new routes in Europe and Asia. Chief operating officer Mark Galardo says the move signals a push to become what he calls a “true global” carrier as the country’s largest airline aims to draw more heavily on higher-margin international customers and less on domestic ones. It also comes as Air Canada and its competitors struggle to navigate higher jet fuel costs amid the Iran war and a prolonged plunge in Canadian demand for U.S. travel. Starting next summer, the airline says it will launch service to foreign cities that include Guangzhou in China, Oslo in Norway and Dubrovnik in Croatia, cementing its status as the second-largest North American carrier by overseas destinations served. Galardo is stressing Canada as an ideal spot for layovers on trips between the Americas and Europe, which make up a key revenue source. Driving the expansion are new long-range Airbus A321 narrow-body jets as well as Boeing 787 wide-bodies, though major delivery delays have hampered their rollout. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026. Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

item.title: Carney says Trump officials shouldn’t comment on Canadian politics
item.description: Amid a breakdown of trade talks and a simmering tariff war between Canada and the United States, Prime Minister Mark Carney says unelected U.S. officials should refrain from commenting on Canadian ...
item.dc:creator: Spencer Van Dyk
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Amid a breakdown of trade talks and a simmering tariff war between Canada and the United States, Prime Minister Mark Carney says unelected U.S. officials should refrain from commenting on Canadian politics. “I don’t think, with all respect, (that) appointed, unelected cabinet members in the United States are experts on Canadian politics,” Carney told reporters following an announcement in Thunder Bay, Ont. on Thursday, when asked about comments by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week. Lutnick denied that U.S. officials were hung up on French-language laws — one of the reported reasons talks collapsed — adding Canada walked away from a deal with the U.S. late last month “for political purposes.” After weeks of intense talks throughout the summer, Canada and the U.S. failed to strike a last-minute trade deal, leading to U.S. President Donald Trump’s new slate of 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods to come into effect. The affected items include those covered under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA). In response, Carney has announced Canada will impose counter-tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of American goods starting Sept. 8. “Everything this government is doing, everything I’m trying to do, is to work with provinces, work with willing partners around the world, work with labour, work with business, to move forward to the benefit of our citizens,” Carney said. “That’s the small p, if you want to call that politics, that’s small p politics,” Carney added, insisting Canadian negotiators are “not positioning on this stuff.” Pointing to the failed deal, which reportedly fell apart at the 11th hour, Carney said the Americans had immovable red lines that Canada couldn’t accept. “Boom it’s in there, you know, our way or the highway, take-it-or-leave it attitude,” Carney said, adding those red lines no longer seem to be there. The prime minister said what U.S. officials now appear to be saying is different from the lines they drew during negotiations. Carney’s comments on Thursday are not the first time he’s publicly taken aim at U.S. negotiators. Speaking to reporters earlier this week, Carney called on them to quit their online attacks and take trade discussions more seriously, saying when they “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious,” Canada will return to the negotiating table. In a post to social media on Thursday, Trump wrote that it is all good for Canadian politicians, namely Carney, to make the U.S. president out to be “the enemy,” until Canada’s “economy collapses.”

item.title: Canada July trade surplus shrinks, weeks before new U.S. tariffs
item.description: Canada’s trade surplus sharply narrowed in July as exports of energy and metal products shrank while imports rose, data showed on Thursday, just weeks before a major escalation in trade dispute with ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Canada’s trade surplus narrowed sharply in July as exports of energy and metal products shrank while imports rose, just weeks before Washington’s new 50 per cent tariffs begin to show up in statistics, posing a stiffer test for Canadian exporters. The trade surplus was $769 million, compared with a four-year high surplus of $4.2 billion posted a month ago, Statistics Canada said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a surplus of $3.57 billion in July. Exports dropped 2.3 per cent, while imports increased 2.2 per cent. Amid an escalating trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, Canada has been seeking to reduce its dependence on its neighbor and largest trading partner. The U.S. accounted for 66.35 per cent of Canada’s total exports in July, down from 69.39 per cent in June and 72.64 per cent a year ago. However, Canada’s import dependence on the U.S. has only narrowed to 59 per cent in the last 12 months compared with 62 per cent in 2024. The July figures, Canada’s fifth consecutive monthly trade surplus, extended a run of relatively resilient Canadian trade despite more than a year and a half of U.S. tariffs. However, Washington’s latest duties, imposed last month, will provide a tougher test for exporters in the coming months. The decrease in exports in July was primarily led by energy products, which account for almost a quarter of Canada’s total exports, and 95 per cent of which usually flow south of the border. Their value dropped 4.4 per cent in July, a third consecutive monthly decline after exports of crude oil decreased by 5.5 per cent, with both prices and volumes falling, StatsCan said. Exports of metal and non-metallic mineral products, which posted an increase of 15.8 per cent in the prior month, also shrank by 8.5 per cent in July. As a result, Canada’s total exports fell to $76.14 billion, down from $77.96 billion in June, but excluding metals and energy, exports increased 0.6 per cent in July. The overall decrease in total exports in July was partially offset by higher exports of aircraft and other transportation equipment and parts, which surged by 34.9 per cent. Imports rose in July to a value of $75.37 billion, up from $73.76 billion, StatsCan said, adding that it was the sixth consecutive monthly increase. This was led by an 11.4 per cent increase in imports of motor vehicles and parts, mainly from the U.S. Exports to the U.S. dropped 6.6 per cent in July while imports from the country increased by 1.8 per cent, shrinking Canada’s trade surplus with its main trading partner by more than 40 per cent to $5.9 billion. Stuart Bergman, chief economist at Export Development Canada, the country’s official export credit agency, said that keeping the share of Canada’s exports going to the U.S. below 70 per cent was an encouraging trend. “Sheer gravity alone pulls exporters to the U.S. market,” Bergman said, but added that there have been concerted efforts to shift some of that gravity to other markets, citing the increase in agricultural exports, especially canola to China and Japan. Year-to-date share of exports to the U.S. is around 68 per cent, down from 73 per cent in the year-ago period. Exports to countries other than the United States rose 7.4 per cent, while imports increased 2.8 per cent, leaving Canada with a non-U.S. trade deficit of $5.1 billion, down from $6.1 billion in the prior month. The Canadian dollar was trading firmer, up 0.35 per cent to $1.3792 against the U.S. dollar, or 72.51 U.S. cents. --- Reporting by Promit Mukherjee; Editing by Dale Smith; Editing by Sharon Singleton

item.title: BRP reports $136.8M second-quarter loss, raises full-year guidance
item.description: BRP Inc. raised its full-year guidance as it reported a loss of $136.8 million in its latest quarter, compared with a profit of $57.1 million a year ago.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: BRP Inc. raised its full-year guidance as it reported a loss of $136.8 million in its latest quarter, compared with a profit of $57.1 million a year ago. The Ski-Doo and Sea-Doo maker says the loss amounted to $1.88 per diluted share for the quarter ended July 31, compared with a profit of 79 cents per share a year earlier. BRP’s normalized result for the quarter amounted to a loss of 18 cents per diluted share, compared with a normalized profit of 92 cents per diluted share a year ago. Revenue for the quarter totalled $2.24 billion, up from $1.89 billion in the same quarter last year. In its outlook for its full year, BRP says it now expects revenue to total between $9.225 billion and $9.475 billion, up from earlier expectations for between $9.125 billion and $9.375 billion. The company also says it now expects normalized earnings between $4 and $4.50 per diluted share for its full year, up from earlier guidance for between $3 and $3.50 per diluted share. BRP’s latest financial results came as the company said Sébastien Martel will step down as chief financial officer and be replaced by Minh Thanh Tran, effective Oct. 1. Martel will serve as an executive adviser to the chief executive until his retirement in April next year. Tran joined BRP in 2017 and has worked across the company including corporate strategy, mergers and acquisitions and product strategy. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.
